questions.topic: What a source-to-sink analysis rule is trying to prove
questions.learningObjective: State the claim a source-to-sink rule makes about a path
questions.stem: A static analysis rule is written to look for an order field that reaches a database call without being validated.

options.text: It is trying to prove that attacker-controlled data can flow to a dangerous operation unchecked.
It is trying to prove that every database call in the program is vulnerable to the same flaw.
options.misconception: treats a flow rule as a whole-program verdict

options.text: It is trying to prove that the order field is stored in the database rather than kept in memory.
options.misconception: confuses flow analysis with storage location

options.text: It is trying to prove that the program was written by someone outside the original team.
options.misconception: reads analysis findings as authorship evidence

questions.explanation: The rule encodes a claim that untrusted data reaches a dangerous operation without passing a check. It says nothing about the rest of the program, so a reported path is a starting point.
questions.hint: Read the rule as a claim about one path.

questions.topic: Why a source-to-sink rule reports things that are not flaws
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a dismissed-path count as a measure of rule noise

options.text: The 12 dismissed paths still count as findings, so the rule's output should always be reported as 40.
options.misconception: counts dismissed paths as real findings

options.text: Twelve of the 40 are dismissed, which is 30 percent, so the rule over-reports on this component.
The rule is precise, because reviewers only dismiss paths that are trivially harmless in practice.
options.misconception: assumes reviewers dismiss only trivial cases

options.text: The 12 dismissed paths show the reviewers were mistaken, so the original 40 findings all stand.
options.misconception: treats reviewer dismissal as reviewer error

questions.explanation: Dismissed paths are the cases where the rule's claim did not hold, so 12 of 40 means the rule over-reports by 30 percent here. The remaining 28 still need their own review before being reported.
questions.hint: Divide the dismissed paths by all reported paths.

questions.topic: What a dynamic test observes that a static one cannot
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a dynamic test can observe that static reasoning cannot
questions.stem: The team compares a static analysis graph of the upload handler with a dynamic test that posts malformed archives.

answer.exemplar: The dynamic test shows what the running program actually did with the malformed archives, including the crashes and the unexpected writes, while the static graph shows the paths the analyst reasoned about ahead of time. A static rule can only report a path visible in the code, so it misses behaviour that depends on timing, on environment, or on values only produced at run time, which is exactly what a dynamic test can expose.

questions.explanation: Static reasoning works from the code, so it can only report paths visible in that code. A dynamic test observes what actually happens at run time, including behaviour no rule could have predicted.
questions.hint: Ask what each method can actually observe.

questions.stem: A coverage graph for a fuzzing run shows 480 edges in the program, and the run has so far covered 300 of them.
questions.explanation: 300 of 480 edges is 62.5 percent, and a coverage-guided fuzzer uses that figure to judge whether it is still learning. If the number stops moving, the run needs new seeds.
questions.hint: Divide covered edges by all edges.

options.text: Coverage rose only 12 edges because the program has 12 reachable branches in total, so the run was complete.

questions.explanation: A fuzzer mutates its corpus to reach new edges, so one input gives it little material. The 12 edges gained in the first hour show it was still building a corpus, so it needed new seeds.

options.text: The judgement says how realistically the flaw can be reached and used, which the score alone does not say.

options.misconception: believes boundaries do not limit a rule

options.text: The 3 boundary calls are errors in the program, so they should be reported as defects in their own right.

questions.topic: What a source-to-sink analysis rule is trying to prove
questions.learningObjective: Describe precisely what a reported taint path establishes
questions.stem: A team is asked to explain what a taint rule establishes when it reports a path from a form field to a shell call.

answer.exemplar: The rule establishes that a path exists in the code from the attacker-supplied field to the shell call, and that no sanitising step is recorded along that path. It does not establish that the path is reachable at run time, that the input really is attacker-controlled in the deployed configuration, or that an attacker would gain anything from running it, so those points must be checked separately before the finding is treated as a real flaw.

questions.explanation: The rule establishes a path and the absence of a recorded check along it. Reachability, real attacker control and the resulting gain are separate questions that the path alone does not answer.
questions.hint: Separate the path from what it implies.

options.text: The fuzzer has crashed, because a stalled coverage graph is the normal sign of a broken harness.

questions.topic: What an exploitability judgement adds to a severity score
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an exploitability judgement contributes to risk handling
questions.stem: A reviewer must explain what an exploitability judgement contributes to a severity score on a raised ticket.

answer.exemplar: The judgement should describe how the flaw could actually be used: what an attacker must already have, whether user interaction is needed, and how much of the affected system the attacker reaches. Severity scores describe potential impact if the flaw is exploited, so adding the judgement tells the reader how likely that impact is to be realised, and it is what turns a long list of high scores into a workable order of work.

questions.explanation: A severity score describes impact, and the exploitability judgement describes how reachable and usable the flaw is in practice. Together they separate the worst case from the likely case.
questions.hint: Say what the judgement tells the reader.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a corpus of one input costs a fuzzer
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a narrow starting corpus slows a campaign
questions.stem: A campaign review asks why beginning with a single input produced a narrow coverage graph in the first hour.

answer.exemplar: The campaign should have started from a corpus of varied seeds, one per input format the parser accepts, so the fuzzer had material to mutate across different branches. With a single seed the fuzzer first spends its budget rediscovering the paths the seed already reaches, and only then begins to differ from it, which is why the first hour produced very little new coverage compared with a campaign that started from a broad corpus.

questions.explanation: A fuzzer advances by mutating its corpus, so a single seed spends early budget rediscovering paths it already reaches. A varied corpus, one per input format, reaches unexplored code sooner.
questions.hint: Ask what a fuzzer needs to reach new code.

questions.stem: A study group compares a static rule with a running test on the same upload handler.

answer.exemplar: The static rule reasons from the source text and can only report a path it can see in the code, including paths that never occur at run time because of the values that reach them. questions.explanation: A static rule works from the source and reports paths it can see, including some that never occur. A running test shows what happens with the inputs it supplies, so the two answer different questions.

options.text: The rule analysed 75 percent of the graph, and the 16 skipped nodes bound what the report can claim.
The rule analysed 48 nodes, so the report overstates the work that was actually done.
options.misconception: confuses node counts with analysis

questions.explanation: 48 of 64 nodes is 75 percent, and the 16 nodes behind unanalysable calls are the boundary of what the report can claim. They are a stated limit on the result, not evidence that those paths are safe.
questions.hint: Divide analysed nodes by all nodes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a source-to-sink analysis rule is trying to prove
questions.learningObjective: Describe a reported path in plain terms without overstating it
questions.stem: A report writer has to describe what a source-to-sink rule establishes in one paragraph for a non-technical reader.

answer.exemplar: The paragraph should say that the tool traced a value taken from something the outside world controls, followed it through the program, and found that it reaches an operation where it could do damage, and that no step on the route was seen to check it first. It should also say clearly that this is a path found in the code and not yet a demonstrated attack, so the reader understands that a person still has to confirm the path can be reached and used.

questions.explanation: A source-to-sink rule establishes a route from untrusted data to a sensitive operation with no recorded check. It does not demonstrate an attack, so a plain description must keep that clear.
questions.hint: Keep the claim and the caveat clear.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a source-to-sink rule reports things that are not flaws
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the dismissed share of a scanner's output
questions.stem: A scanner's findings graph for the reporting service shows 160 paths, and the review dismisses 48 of them.
questions.explanation: 48 of 160 paths is 30 percent, and each dismissed path shows the rule's claim did not hold. A third of the output being noise means the rule needs tuning or triage in front of the queue.
questions.hint: Divide dismissed paths by all reported paths.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a dynamic test observes that a static one cannot
questions.learningObjective: Compare the paths covered by a static pass and a dynamic pass

stimulus.body: The static pass over the queue worker produced 9 findings, all of them paths from a message field to a log write. The dynamic pass sent 5,000 malformed messages and triggered 2 crashes inside the worker before it ever reached the logging code.

questions.stem: What does the pair report indicate about the two passes?

options.text: The dynamic pass saw failures on a path the static findings did not describe, so the static set missed it.
The static pass was more thorough, because it produced 9 findings against the dynamic pass's 2 crashes.
options.misconception: counts findings against crashes as thoroughness

options.text: The dynamic pass is unreliable, because crashes during testing are normal for any service.
options.misconception: dismisses crashes as normal

options.text: Both passes agree the problem is in the logging code, because the static findings all point there.
options.misconception: forces agreement between the passes

questions.explanation: The dynamic pass recorded failures on a route the static findings never described, the gap between methods. The static set may be right about its paths, but it missed the behaviour that broke it.
questions.hint: Compare the paths each pass covered.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a coverage-guided fuzzer needs a measure of progress
questions.learningObjective: Decide what a stalled coverage graph means for a campaign budget
questions.stem: A campaign's coverage graph shows 900 edges, 400 reached, and the run has been going for 30 minutes with no change for the last 10.

options.text: The campaign is complete, because the graph has stopped changing and the program cannot be reached further.
options.misconception: treats a plateau as completeness

options.text: The campaign is broken, because a healthy coverage-guided fuzzer adds edges every minute.
options.misconception: assumes constant coverage growth

options.text: The run has stopped gaining coverage, so it needs new seeds or a restart to reach the remaining edges.
The campaign is fine, because 400 edges out of 900 is already most of what any campaign reaches.
options.misconception: assumes 44 percent is a normal ceiling

questions.explanation: First read the graph: 400 of 900 edges and no movement for ten minutes means the fuzzer is finding no new paths. Then new seeds or a restart are needed to reach unseen code.
questions.hint: Check whether the graph still moves.
